talks.title: Unsecurity Episode 261: CMMC Delay and Compliance Costs with Eric Vollbrecht and Nathan Austin
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Unsecurity Episode 261: CMMC Delay and Compliance Costs with Eric Vollbrecht and Nathan Austin.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Brad and Megan Larkins host Eric Vollbrecht (Senior Security Consultant) and Nathan Austin from Mytech's CMMC team on the Unsecurity Podcast to discuss the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC). The episode examines recent regulatory shifts, including the Department of Defense's 60-day pause on CMMC Phase 2 third-party assessment deadlines, alongside heightened Department of Justice enforcement under the False Claims Act. The panel provides a realistic, transparent breakdown of compliance timelines, preparation costs, and common operational pitfalls faced by small-to-medium businesses in the defense industrial base.

Key Topics:
- Pentagon's 60-day review and pause on CMMC Phase 2 third-party certification deadlines
- Heightened False Claims Act enforcement and civil fraud penalties for false self-attestations
- Real-world financial cost modeling: gap assessments, readiness consulting, and technical debt
- Scoping Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI), SPRS scoring, and vetting MSP partners

Technical Details:
The discussion centers on the Pentagon's announcement suspending CMMC Phase 2 third-party assessment requirements for a 60-day review period, driven largely by a severe shortage of certified third-party assessment organizations (C3PAOs) and industry cost concerns. The hosts emphasize that while third-party audits are paused, underlying requirements—including self-attestation against NIST SP 800-171 and reporting into the Supplier Performance Risk System (SPRS)—remain active. Crucially, the Department of Justice has expanded attorney staffing to prosecute cybersecurity fraud under the False Claims Act. Nathan cites a recent enforcement action where a contractor falsely self-attested their SPRS score, claiming compliance despite scoring between negative 200 and positive 10, resulting in a civil settlement exceeding $500,000. Under CMMC Level 2, contractors must fully achieve all 110 controls with zero exceptions, eliminating historical leniency.

The speakers outline the true financial and logistical scope of achieving compliance, contrasting realistic multi-phase roadmaps against fraudulent providers advertising "$5,000 in six weeks" certifications. They detail the abrupt collapse of a major private-equity-backed CMMC MSP in May, which left clients stranded without global administrator access to their environments. A legitimate compliance lifecycle spans 12 to 18 months and entails three primary cost phases: an initial gap assessment ($10,000 to $20,000, averaging ~$15,000), readiness preparation covering policy generation, log collection, and control implementation ($20,000 to $60,000), and formal C3PAO auditing fees ($40,000+). Factoring in technical debt—such as deploying dedicated CUI cloud enclaves, server hardware refreshes, and migrating to Microsoft GCC High licensing—first-year compliance expenditures typically total between $100,000 and $200,000.

Key Takeaways:
Contractors in the defense industrial base should not interpret regulatory delays as a reprieve from cybersecurity accountability, particularly given active False Claims Act investigations targeting dishonest self-attestations. Organizations must establish an accurate scope of CUI environments and recognize that compliance requires continuous evidence collection rather than one-time paperwork. Executive leadership must perform diligent vetting of consulting partners, budgeting realistically for technical debt remediation and ongoing compliance maintenance across the three-year certification cycle.

talks.title: Unsecurity Episode 260: Women in Cybersecurity with Mea Yang
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Unsecurity Episode 260: Women in Cybersecurity with Mea Yang.
talks.summary:
Episode Context

Hosts Megan Lkins and Brad Nye welcome FRSecure consultant Mia Yang for a conversation on women in cybersecurity, recorded after a publishing backlog delayed recent Unsecurity episodes. The episode opens with light hobby talk—gardening, games, and moving—before shifting to industry inclusion.

Talent Shortage Versus Identification

Mia argues the decade-long “cyber talent shortage” narrative reflects an identification problem, not missing people. Organizations seek narrow profiles, negotiate against their interests, and fail to recognize capable candidates already available, including women who have not “disappeared.”

Pipeline and Culture Drop-Off

Discussion references Heroic Hacks speakers noting strong girl participation through high school, then steep attrition afterward. The hosts frame this as cultural expectation rather than lack of interest or ability—environment and messaging matter more than raw aptitude.

Inclusive Hiring Perspective

The panel urges holistic funnel thinking: fix how roles are defined, how candidates are evaluated, and how inclusive cultures retain diverse talent instead of repeating the same shortage headlines.

talks.title: Unsecurity Episode 259: The Cyber Resilience Act, Open Source, & AI w/ Madalin Neag & CRob
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Unsecurity Episode 259: The Cyber Resilience Act, Open Source, & AI w/ Madalin Neag & CRob.
talks.summary:
Podcast setup

On Unsecurity, Megan Lurkins hosts OpenSSF EU policy adviser Maline and CTO Christopher Robinson (Crob) to explain the EU Cyber Resilience Act for listeners unfamiliar with the regulation.

CRA scope and timeline

Maline describes CRA as broad horizontal legislation requiring secure-by-design digital products across their lifecycle, replacing narrower radio-equipment rules. Full applicability arrives 11 December next year with some obligations from 11 September this year, affecting any manufacturer placing products on the EU market regardless of headquarters.

Awareness gap

OpenSSF surveyed over one thousand companies and found sixty-six percent unaware of CRA despite imminent deadlines. Robinson notes open source underpins an estimated nine trillion dollars of economic value and that CRA codifies long-standing AppSec expectations—secure development, vulnerability handling, and accountability—now as law rather than voluntary guidance.

talks.title: Unsecurity Episode 258: The CISSP Mentor Program with Brian Kelley
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Unsecurity Episode 258: The CISSP Mentor Program with Brian Kelley.
talks.summary:
Overview:
In episode 258 of the Unsecurity podcast, hosts Brad Nigh and Megan Larkins interview Brian Kelley, a cybersecurity consultant at FRSecure, regarding the structure, evolution, and pedagogical impact of FRSecure's free CISSP Mentor Program. Kelley shares his career journey transitioning from managed service provider (MSP) systems administration into security consulting, detailing how structured certification preparation bridges technical expertise and organizational risk management. The discussion explores modern instructional design for infosec certifications, study strategies, and exam psychology.

Key Topics:
- FRSecure CISSP Mentor Program curriculum and structure
- Career pivoting from IT/MSP systems administration to cybersecurity consulting
- Evolution from synchronous lecturing to flipped classroom instructional models
- Pedagogical frameworks for mastering the eight CISSP Common Body of Knowledge (CBK) domains

Technical Details:
Brian Kelley outlines the design and operational methodology of FRSecure's annual, community-focused CISSP Mentor Program. Originally delivered as four hours of weekly synchronous live lectures, the program transitioned to a flipped classroom model to enhance student comprehension and retention. Under this framework, students consume asynchronous pre-recorded instructional modules covering the eight CISSP CBK domains on their own schedule, reserving two weekly live hours exclusively for interactive panel discussions, real-world case breakdowns, and open Q&A sessions.

Kelley details how the program utilizes a dedicated Discord community to sustain student engagement throughout the multi-month course. Mentors post daily scenario-based "question of the day" drills, prompting candidates to analyze operational security dilemmas through the lens of a senior risk advisor or CISO rather than a hands-on systems administrator. The pedagogical sequence intentionally frontloads foundational governance, risk management, and compliance principles before diving into technical domains like cryptography, network security architecture, and software development security. This structural approach conditions technical professionals from IT and MSP backgrounds to unlearn reactive troubleshooting habits and prioritize business impact, policy alignment, and risk mitigation.

The discussion also emphasizes cognitive conditioning and exam preparation mechanics. Candidates are coached on reading comprehension strategies to deconstruct tricky exam phrasing, manage time constraints across the computerized adaptive testing (CAT) format, and schedule hard testing deadlines to enforce study discipline. Kelley and the hosts stress holistic lifestyle conditioning, including adequate sleep, proper nutrition, and cognitive pacing leading up to exam day.

Key Takeaways:
Succeeding on the CISSP exam requires candidates to transition from technical, tactical problem-solving to strategic, risk-based management decision-making. Adopting a flipped classroom instructional model combining asynchronous deep dives with interactive peer discussions significantly boosts knowledge retention and conceptual application. Setting firm exam target dates and engaging in continuous scenario-based question analysis are critical factors for successfully passing advanced professional certification exams.
